### Question 78 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Divide the global linked list into several independent sub‑lists, protect each sub‑list with its own mutex (or read‑write lock), and assign threads to work on different sub‑lists; this reduces lock contention enough to meet the 3× speedup while preserving correctness.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Protect the entire linked list with a single global mutex; this will guarantee thread safety and is sufficient to reach the required 3× throughput on an 8‑core processor. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A single global mutex does guarantee mutual exclusion, but it serializes all list operations, causing the threads to contend heavily for the same lock. On an 8‑core machine the contention will typically prevent any substantial speedup, let alone the 3× target, because most of the work becomes effectively single‑threaded.

**Option:** Replace the linked list with a fixed‑size array and use lock‑free atomic primitives for all updates; no explicit synchronization is needed, and the program will automatically achieve the desired performance. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While lock‑free algorithms can reduce contention, converting a linked list to an array is not trivial when the data set size is dynamic, and atomic primitives alone do not eliminate the need for careful design to avoid ABA problems or memory reclamation issues. Moreover, without proper partitioning, atomics can still become a bottleneck, making the 3× throughput goal unlikely.

**Option:** Divide the global linked list into several independent sub‑lists, protect each sub‑list with its own mutex (or read‑write lock), and assign threads to work on different sub‑lists; this reduces lock contention enough to meet the 3× speedup while preserving correctness. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. By partitioning the data structure, each thread contends only for the lock protecting its own sub‑list, dramatically lowering synchronization overhead compared with a single lock. The reduced contention allows multiple cores to make progress simultaneously, making the 3× throughput improvement on an 8‑core system achievable while still ensuring that all reads and writes remain thread‑safe.

**Option:** Store a complete copy of the linked list in thread‑local storage for each worker thread and merge the results after processing; this eliminates all race conditions without any synchronization cost. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Making a full copy per thread defeats the purpose of a shared global list, leading to excessive memory usage and duplicated work, especially with large financial transaction volumes. The merge step would re‑introduce synchronization and could become a new bottleneck, making the approach both inefficient and unlikely to meet the performance target.

**Option:** Register a pthread_atfork() handler that resets the global list before each thread begins execution; this guarantees safe concurrent access during the ETL pipeline. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. The pthread_atfork() handler runs only in the child process after a fork, not for threads created with pthread_create, so it does not address concurrent access in a multithreaded program. Consequently, race conditions on the linked list would remain, and the handler provides no performance benefit.

**Option:** Declare the global list pointer as volatile; this ensures that all threads see the most recent updates without needing locks, giving both correctness and the required speedup. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. The volatile qualifier only prevents certain compiler optimizations; it does not provide atomicity or memory‑ordering guarantees required for safe concurrent modification. Without proper locking or lock‑free synchronization, data races can corrupt the list, leading to undefined behavior and no guaranteed performance improvement.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of thread safety, lock contention, and scalable data‑structure design in C. The correct approach is to reduce contention by partitioning the shared structure and protecting each partition with its own lock, which allows multiple cores to work in parallel and can achieve the desired 3× speedup. Common misconceptions include believing that a single global lock or volatile qualifier can both protect data and deliver high performance, or that lock‑free atomics or thread‑local copies automatically solve concurrency problems without trade‑offs. In practice, developers must balance correctness (using appropriate synchronization) with scalability (minimizing critical‑section duration), often by using fine‑grained locking or lock‑free algorithms suited to the workload. Remember that any synchronization primitive introduces overhead, so the granularity of protection should match the contention profile of the application.

### Question 79 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Separate per‑thread buffers that are flushed in batches at regular intervals.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** A single lock‑free ring buffer shared by all producer threads. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Although a lock‑free ring buffer avoids kernel‑level locks, all producers still compete on the same atomic indices, which at 10 M packets/s creates severe CAS contention and can easily exceed the 5 µs budget. In addition, if the buffer becomes full during bursts, producers may have to retry, risking missed entries or increased latency.

**Option:** A mutex‑protected circular buffer accessed by all producers. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A mutex introduces kernel‑mode context switches and serializes access, causing contention that far exceeds the allowed overhead for a 10 M‑packet workload. Real‑world tests show mutex‑protected logging becomes a bottleneck, and any contention can lead to packet‑processing stalls, violating the performance requirement.

**Option:** Separate per‑thread buffers that are flushed in batches at regular intervals. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. By giving each producer its own private buffer, there is no inter‑thread contention, and writing a log entry is just a simple memory store, keeping the per‑packet cost well under 5 µs. Periodic batch flushing transfers the accumulated entries to the shared log without impacting the fast path, and as long as the buffers are sized to avoid overflow, no log entry is lost.

**Option:** A hybrid scheme where each thread writes to its own lock‑free ring buffer and a dedicated consumer thread merges the entries into a global log. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is plausible but not the best choice. While it eliminates direct contention among producers, the extra consumer thread adds complexity and introduces latency in the merge step, which can jeopardize the strict 5 µs budget under peak load. Moreover, if the consumer cannot keep up, individual per‑thread buffers may overflow, risking loss of log entries.

**Option:** A lock‑free ring buffer combined with a drop‑on‑full policy that discards the oldest entries when the buffer is full. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because it violates the requirement that no log entry be lost. A drop‑on‑full policy intentionally discards data to maintain throughput, which is unacceptable for a logging subsystem that must preserve every timestamped event. Even if performance meets the 5 µs limit, the loss of information makes this configuration unsuitable.

**Option:** A global log buffer protected by a spin‑lock taken for each log entry. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Spin‑locks may appear lightweight, but at 10 M packets per second many threads will repeatedly spin, wasting CPU cycles and inflating the per‑packet overhead well beyond the 5 µs ceiling. Additionally, excessive spinning can starve other cores and degrade overall system throughput, contradicting the design goals.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests the learner's understanding of high‑performance concurrent logging techniques and the trade‑offs between contention, latency, and data safety. Per‑thread buffers with periodic batch flushing (option 3) eliminate inter‑thread contention, keep the critical logging path extremely cheap, and, when sized properly, guarantee that no entry is overwritten or dropped, satisfying both the performance and reliability constraints. Options that share a single data structure (options 1, 2, 4, and 6) introduce contention or additional latency that cannot meet the 5 µs budget at 10 M packets/s. Option 5 explicitly trades correctness for speed, breaking the no‑loss requirement. In real‑world systems, designers often employ thread‑local logging buffers combined with background aggregation to achieve deterministic, low‑overhead logging without sacrificing completeness.

### Question 80 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Run the program under a memory error detector such as Address Sanitizer or Valgrind to pinpoint the use‑after‑free.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Restart the application immediately and monitor for recurrence. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is not the correct first action. Restarting only masks the problem and does not give any insight into why the use‑after‑free is happening. Without additional diagnostics you are likely to see the same crash again, and the underlying data corruption risk remains.

**Option:** Add a global mutex to serialize all access between the two worker threads. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** While serializing the threads might prevent the race condition, blindly adding a global lock is a heavy‑handed fix that can degrade performance and may not address the root cause. The fault is a use‑after‑free, which often stems from mismatched allocation/free patterns rather than a simple data race. Proper investigation is needed before introducing such a coarse synchronization mechanism.

**Option:** Run the program under a memory error detector such as Address Sanitizer or Valgrind to pinpoint the use‑after‑free. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This is the correct first step. Tools like ASAN or Valgrind instrument the binary and report the exact location where freed memory is later accessed, giving you a reproducible stack trace. With that information you can fix the allocation/free logic before any further data corruption occurs, which is essential for a financial transaction system.

**Option:** Increase the malloc arena size to reduce the chance of heap reuse. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Changing the heap configuration might delay the reuse of freed blocks, but it does not solve the fundamental bug of accessing memory after it has been freed. The problem will eventually reappear, and such tuning is a band‑aid rather than a root‑cause fix. Moreover, it can increase memory consumption unnecessarily on a production server.

**Option:** Replace the freed pointer with NULL after each free to prevent dangling references. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Setting a pointer to NULL after free is a good defensive habit, but it does not guarantee safety in a multithreaded context where another thread may have already copied the pointer value. The crash indicates that some thread is still using the original pointer, and merely null‑ing the original variable will not affect copies held elsewhere. Thus it is not sufficient as a first investigative step.

**Option:** Deploy a newer version of the OS kernel assuming the bug is kernel‑related. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Kernel bugs are unlikely to manifest as a use‑after‑free of a heap pointer inside a user‑space application. Updating the kernel would consume valuable change‑management resources without addressing the actual cause. The correct approach is to focus on the application’s memory handling first.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The scenario tests the ability to prioritize systematic debugging of memory errors in a concurrent C program. The core dump already identifies a use‑after‑free, so the most effective first action is to run the program under a memory‑error detection tool such as Address Sanitizer or Valgrind, which will pinpoint the exact code path that accesses the freed block. Common misconceptions include treating the symptom (the crash) as the problem by restarting the service, or applying coarse synchronisation or configuration tweaks without understanding the underlying bug. Defensive coding practices like nulling freed pointers are beneficial but do not replace a thorough investigation. In production systems handling financial data, eliminating use‑after‑free bugs before any data corruption occurs is critical, and memory sanitizers provide the quickest, most reliable way to locate and fix them.

### Question 81 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Implement lock‑free insertion at the head using atomic compare‑and‑swap on the head pointer.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Replace the mutex with a spinlock that only protects the head pointer update. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A spinlock still serializes all insertions and can waste CPU cycles under heavy contention, leading to the same corruption if the critical section is not correctly limited. Moreover, merely changing the lock type does not address the underlying race condition caused by improper protection of the linked‑list pointers.

**Option:** Use a read‑write lock, taking a write lock for insertions and a read lock for traversals. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Insertions at the head are write operations, and read‑write locks do not give any advantage when writes dominate the workload, as they still require exclusive access. The high insertion rate would cause writers to constantly block readers, and the corruption would likely remain because the lock still covers the whole list instead of just the head update.

**Option:** Implement lock‑free insertion at the head using atomic compare‑and‑swap on the head pointer. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. A lock‑free algorithm using an atomic compare‑and‑swap can safely add a node at the head without holding a coarse‑grained mutex, eliminating contention and protecting against race conditions even at 50,000 inserts per second. Real‑world systems such as the Linux kernel's RCU lists use similar techniques to achieve high‑throughput, low‑latency updates.

**Option:** Keep the existing mutex but increase its priority to avoid priority inversion. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Raising the mutex's priority may help with priority inversion but does not eliminate the fundamental race condition caused by insufficient protection of the list pointers. The corruption stems from concurrent modifications, not from scheduler priority issues, so this change would not resolve the data integrity problem.

**Option:** Serialize all operations by moving the list to a single‑threaded event loop. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While serialization would prevent concurrent access, it defeats the purpose of a multithreaded packet buffer and would dramatically reduce throughput, making the system unable to handle 50,000 inserts per second. The requirement is to maintain high concurrency, not to eliminate it.

**Option:** Add a second mutex to protect the tail pointer, leaving the head protected by the original mutex. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Corruption occurs during head insertions, so protecting the tail pointer is irrelevant. Introducing an extra mutex adds complexity and potential deadlocks without addressing the race condition affecting the head of the list.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of high‑performance concurrent data‑structure design, specifically how to avoid race conditions in a doubly linked list when many threads insert at the head. The best solution is a lock‑free insertion using atomic compare‑and‑swap, which provides safe, contention‑free updates to the head pointer. Common misconceptions include thinking that simply switching to a spinlock or a read‑write lock improves concurrency; these still serialize writes and can waste CPU cycles. Raising mutex priority or adding unrelated locks does not fix the underlying race, and moving to a single‑threaded model sacrifices the required throughput. In production network code, lock‑free techniques or fine‑grained synchronization are the preferred patterns for scalable packet buffering.

### Question 82 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Declare the counter, configuration struct, and work‑queue pointer as static file‑scope variables, protect every access with a single pthread_mutex_t also declared static, and expose only opaque functions in the public header.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Declare the counter, configuration struct, and work‑queue pointer as static file‑scope variables, protect every access with a single pthread_mutex_t also declared static, and expose only opaque functions in the public header. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. Static file‑scope variables have internal linkage, so they cannot be referenced outside the library source file, fulfilling the encapsulation requirement. A single mutex serializes all accesses, guaranteeing thread‑safety for up to 64 concurrent threads, and keeping the implementation details hidden behind an opaque API preserves the library’s internal state from the applications.

**Option:** Declare the internal state as extern variables in a header so applications can link to them, and protect accesses with atomic_* operations only, without any mutex. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Using extern variables makes the state globally visible, violating the requirement that applications cannot access or modify it. While atomic operations are useful for simple scalars, they do not safely guard complex structures like a configuration struct or a dynamically allocated queue, leading to race conditions in a multithreaded environment.

**Option:** Store each thread’s copy of the counter in thread‑local storage (__thread), keep the configuration struct global, and protect the work queue with a binary semaphore. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A thread‑local counter means the threads do not share a single count, which defeats the purpose of a common library counter. Mixing thread‑local storage with a global configuration and a semaphore introduces unnecessary complexity and still leaves the global configuration exposed to callers, breaking encapsulation.

**Option:** Export the full definition of the configuration struct in the public API, allocate the work queue in the client code and pass a pointer to the library, and use a read‑write lock (pthread_rwlock_t) for the counter only. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Exposing the struct definition allows applications to manipulate the configuration directly, violating the library’s encapsulation. Delegating allocation of the work queue to the client gives the client the ability to modify the queue, which the library is supposed to protect. Additionally, protecting only the counter with a rwlock does not guard the queue or configuration struct from concurrent modifications.

**Option:** Use a single pthread_mutex_t created at library load time, but keep the internal variables as static inside each public function (i. e., as function‑scope static). [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Function‑scope static variables are isolated to each function; they cannot be shared across different functions, so the counter, configuration, and queue would not be visible to all library routines that need them. Consequently, the library would be unable to maintain a coherent shared state, and the mutex would protect only the function that created it, not the whole library state.

**Option:** Implement the library as a set of inline functions in a header file, with the internal state kept in a static variable inside the header, and rely on the compiler’s -fno-common option for thread safety. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Inline functions in a header cause each translation unit that includes the header to get its own copy of the static variable, resulting in separate instances of the internal state rather than a single shared state. Even with -fno-common, the separate copies remain, breaking both encapsulation and thread safety, because modifications in one application will not be visible to another.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of how to keep library state private while providing thread‑safe access in a C environment. The correct solution uses static file‑scope variables, which give the state internal linkage so applications cannot directly reference it, and a single static mutex to serialize all interactions, ensuring safety for up to 64 threads. Common misconceptions include believing that extern variables or thread‑local storage can maintain privacy or that atomic operations alone are sufficient for complex data structures. Exposing structs or delegating memory management to callers also breaks encapsulation and can introduce race conditions. Best practice is to hide all mutable state behind an opaque API, protect it with appropriate synchronization primitives, and avoid leaking implementation details through headers.

### Question 83 Explanation

**Correct Answers:**
1. Implement the buffer as a lock‑free multi‑producer single‑consumer ring using stdatomic operations on head and tail indices.

2. Allocate the circular buffer and any auxiliary structures at program start with static arrays, avoiding any malloc or free calls during processing.

3. Pad the head and tail index variables to separate cache lines to eliminate false sharing between producer and consumer cores.

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Implement the buffer as a lock‑free multi‑producer single‑consumer ring using stdatomic operations on head and tail indices. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. A lock‑free ring buffer allows producers and the consumer to advance their indices without taking a blocking mutex, guaranteeing that each operation completes in bounded time. Using C11 stdatomic ensures proper memory ordering on all supported architectures, which is essential for deterministic latency in a real‑time pipeline.

**Option:** Protect the entire buffer with a single pthread mutex that all producers and the consumer lock before each access. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A single mutex serializes all accesses, turning concurrent writes into a contended critical section that can block for an indeterminate period, violating the 100 µs deadline. Moreover, under high producer load the mutex can cause priority inversion unless additional complex mechanisms are added, which defeats the goal of simplicity and determinism.

**Option:** Allocate the circular buffer and any auxiliary structures at program start with static arrays, avoiding any malloc or free calls during processing. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. By pre‑allocating all memory, the system eliminates the non‑deterministic allocation time and fragmentation that dynamic memory introduces, satisfying the zero‑dynamic‑allocation requirement. Static allocation also allows the compiler to place data in known sections, aiding cache‑friendly layout and simplifying analysis of worst‑case execution time.

**Option:** Use the volatile qualifier on the head and tail variables to guarantee they are read from memory each time. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. The volatile keyword only prevents certain compiler optimizations; it does not provide atomicity, memory ordering, or prevent race conditions. Correct synchronization must rely on atomics or locks; using volatile alone can lead to subtle data corruption in a multi‑threaded environment.

**Option:** Pad the head and tail index variables to separate cache lines to eliminate false sharing between producer and consumer cores. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. False sharing occurs when distinct variables that are frequently updated by different cores reside on the same cache line, causing cache‑line ping‑pong and unpredictable latencies. By aligning and padding the indices to distinct cache lines, each core can update its own variable without evicting the other's data, improving deterministic timing.

**Option:** Set the producer and consumer threads to the default time‑sharing scheduler (SCHED_OTHER) and rely on the OS to meet the 100 µs deadline. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. The standard time‑sharing scheduler makes no guarantees about execution latency; the OS may preempt the threads at any moment, causing missed deadlines. Real‑time applications typically require SCHED_FIFO or SCHED_RR with explicit priorities to obtain bounded response times.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of designing a deterministic, lock‑free producer/consumer pipeline in C. Correct solutions involve a lock‑free ring buffer (option 1) to avoid blocking, static allocation of all data structures (option 3) to eliminate unpredictable allocation latency, and cache‑line padding (option 5) to prevent false sharing that can wreck timing guarantees. The incorrect options are common misconceptions: using a single mutex (option 2) introduces unbounded blocking, declaring shared indices volatile (option 4) does not provide the needed atomic synchronization, and relying on the default scheduler (option 6) cannot assure the hard deadline. In practice, engineers combine these techniques with real‑time scheduling policies and careful profiling to meet strict latency budgets.

### Question 84 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Allocate a separate per‑core ring buffer in thread‑local storage, sized so that the sum of all buffers stays within the 256 MB budget.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Allocate a separate per‑core ring buffer in thread‑local storage, sized so that the sum of all buffers stays within the 256 MB budget. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. By giving each core its own private ring buffer, you eliminate inter‑core contention entirely, satisfying the zero‑contention requirement. Using thread‑local storage also keeps allocation overhead low and allows you to calculate the per‑core buffer size so the total memory does not exceed 256 MB. In practice, this redesign is the first tangible step toward a scalable multicore packet processor.

**Option:** Protect the existing global ring buffer with a single mutex to serialize access across cores. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Although a mutex would make the shared buffer thread‑safe, it introduces serialization that defeats the zero‑contention goal and can become a performance bottleneck under high packet rates. Additionally, keeping the buffer global does not address the memory budget split across cores. Real‑world systems often see massive latency penalties when a single lock guards a high‑throughput data path.

**Option:** Increase the heap size to 512 MB so each core can have its own copy of the original global buffer. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Expanding the heap to 512 MB violates the strict 256 MB memory budget and would likely cause allocation failures on resource‑constrained systems. Moreover, simply duplicating the same global buffer does not remove contention; each core would still need to coordinate access. In production environments, exceeding memory limits can lead to swapping or crashes, especially on embedded network appliances.

**Option:** Convert the global ring buffer into a lock‑free queue using atomic operations while keeping it shared among all cores. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A lock‑free queue reduces some overhead compared to a mutex, but the data structure remains shared, so false sharing and cache‑coherency traffic can still cause contention. Implementing a correct lock‑free queue for a high‑throughput packet path is complex and error‑prone, and it does not guarantee zero contention. Many engineers mistakenly think lock‑free equals contention‑free, which is not true for shared memory accesses.

**Option:** Move the entire packet processor back to a single core to avoid multithreading complexities. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Re‑centralizing the workload on one core directly contradicts the requirement to exploit multiple cores for higher throughput. It also wastes the available hardware resources and does not solve the memory budgeting problem. While simplifying design, this approach would likely result in missed performance targets in real network environments.

**Option:** Profile the current implementation to measure cache‑miss rates before making any architectural changes. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect as the first action. Profiling is valuable for later optimization, but the immediate architectural constraint—zero contention and a strict memory budget—must be addressed before performance tuning. Starting with profiling would delay the essential redesign of the data structure and could lead to wasted effort on a design that will later need a complete overhaul. In practice, designers first ensure the high‑level architecture meets functional constraints, then fine‑tune performance.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests the learner's understanding of how to redesign shared data structures for a multicore, low‑contention environment under a strict memory limit. The correct first step is to replace the global ring buffer with per‑core private buffers so each core can operate independently without synchronization overhead, and to size those buffers to stay within the 256 MB budget. Common misconceptions include thinking that a mutex or lock‑free algorithm will eliminate contention, that simply increasing memory solves the problem, or that profiling should precede architectural changes. Each of those distractors reflects a typical but flawed approach: serialization hurts throughput, larger memory breaches constraints, lock‑free structures remain shared, and profiling does not address the fundamental design requirement. The best practice is to redesign the data structures to be thread‑local early in the migration, then address performance tuning, cache behavior, and further refinements.

### Question 85 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Missing or incorrect memory barriers when accessing lock‑free shared data structures, allowing reorderings that break coherence across cores.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Missing or incorrect memory barriers when accessing lock‑free shared data structures, allowing reorderings that break coherence across cores. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. On ARM, the memory model permits substantial reordering of loads and stores unless explicit barriers (e. g., dmb, smp_mb()) are used. When lock‑free structures are updated without those barriers, one core may see stale or partially updated data, leading to intermittent memory corruption under high contention. In real‑world kernel code, failing to place appropriate barriers around atomic updates is a frequent source of hard‑to‑reproduce bugs.

**Option:** Using spinlocks instead of mutexes, causing priority inversion and occasional deadlocks under real‑time scheduling. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While spinlocks can cause priority inversion on a real‑time kernel, they do not directly corrupt memory; they merely affect scheduling behaviour. The problem description states that all standard mutexes are correctly placed, and the corruption occurs only under heavy multi‑core load, which points away from lock type mismatches. Misusing spinlocks would more likely manifest as hangs, not silent data corruption.

**Option:** False sharing of cache lines between threads, leading to performance degradation but not memory corruption. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. False sharing results in excessive cache‑coherency traffic and can degrade performance, especially with many threads, but it does not corrupt the contents of memory. The symptoms described involve actual corruption of data structures, which false sharing cannot produce. Learners often confuse performance issues with correctness problems, but cache line contention alone cannot change data values.

**Option:** Using a 32‑bit integer to store a pointer on a 64‑bit ARM architecture, causing truncation and occasional crashes. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. The scenario mentions a multi‑core ARM server running a real‑time Linux kernel, which is typically 64‑bit; however, the bug appears only under heavy thread load, not immediately at module load time. Truncating a pointer would cause immediate crashes or kernel oopses, not intermittent corruption that only shows up with many threads. It is a common misconception that pointer size issues manifest only under load, but they are deterministic.

**Option:** Performing non‑atomic 64‑bit loads and stores on a 32‑bit ARM core without using ldrexd/strexd primitives. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect for this specific context. The server is described as a multi‑core ARM server, which in modern production environments is usually 64‑bit, allowing native atomic 64‑bit accesses. Even on a 32‑bit core, the kernel would typically use the provided atomic APIs; if it did not, the corruption would be observable even with a single thread, not only under >64 threads. Hence, this is a plausible sounding distractor but does not match the given constraints.

**Option:** Kernel preemption causing a race condition in code that assumes non‑preemptible context despite holding a mutex. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While kernel preemption can introduce subtle races, a mutex already disables preemption on the holding core for the protected critical section. Moreover, the problem statement confirms that mutexes are correctly placed, so preemption would not bypass the mutual exclusion. The intermittent corruption tied to high thread counts points more toward memory‑ordering issues than to preemption timing.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of memory ordering and the need for explicit barriers when lock‑free data structures are shared across CPU cores, especially on ARM's weak memory model. Correctly placed mutexes guard critical sections, but they do not protect lock‑free paths; without dmb/smp_mb() calls, loads and stores can be reordered, leading to stale or partially updated data and causing intermittent corruption under heavy concurrency. Options such as spinlock misuse, false sharing, pointer truncation, non‑atomic 64‑bit accesses, and kernel preemption are plausible sounding but each addresses a different symptom (deadlocks, performance loss, crashes, deterministic bugs, or scheduling issues) and does not explain the observed pattern. Learners should remember that on weakly ordered architectures, any communication that bypasses traditional locking must be accompanied by the appropriate memory barriers or atomic primitives. Following best practices—using the kernel's atomic APIs, inserting memory barriers where needed, and verifying cache‑line alignment—helps prevent these subtle multi‑core bugs.

### Question 86 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Apply a release‑store to the tail index after writing a message and an acquire‑load to the tail index before reading, which guarantees the consumer sees the fully‑written data on weakly‑ordered architectures.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Apply a release‑store to the tail index after writing a message and an acquire‑load to the tail index before reading, which guarantees the consumer sees the fully‑written data on weakly‑ordered architectures. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is correct. A release store publishes the new tail value only after the payload has been fully written, and an acquire load on the consumer side ensures that any subsequent reads of the payload observe the writes performed before the release. Without these ordering guarantees, a weakly‑ordered CPU could reorder the stores and the consumer might read stale or partially written data, leading to the observed corruption.

**Option:** Declare the ring‑buffer indices as volatile and rely on the compiler to insert the necessary memory fences, eliminating the need for explicit atomic operations. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is incorrect. The `volatile` qualifier only prevents certain compiler optimizations; it does not impose any hardware memory ordering guarantees on weakly‑ordered CPUs. Consequently, even with `volatile`, stores to the payload could be reordered after the index update, causing the consumer to read an incompletely written message.

**Option:** Wrap each write and read operation with a pthread mutex, even though only one thread accesses each side, to avoid data races. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is incorrect. While using a mutex would serialize access and eliminate data races, it introduces significant overhead and lock contention, destroying the ability to achieve 5 million messages per second with sub‑10 µs latency. The single‑producer/single‑consumer pattern can be implemented lock‑free with proper memory ordering, making a mutex unnecessary and detrimental to performance.

**Option:** Pad the head and tail indices to separate cache lines to prevent false sharing, which alone ensures correct ordering on all CPUs. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is partially correct about false‑sharing mitigation but wrong about ordering. Padding eliminates cache‑line thrashing, improving throughput, yet it does not provide the acquire/release semantics required on weakly‑ordered architectures. Without explicit memory barriers, the consumer may still see stale data despite the padding.

**Option:** Assume that because there is only one producer and one consumer, no memory ordering primitives are required; the hardware will naturally serialize the accesses. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is incorrect. Even with a single producer and consumer, weakly‑ordered CPUs (e. g., ARM, Power PC) may reorder writes to different locations, so the index update can become visible before the payload is fully written. Ignoring ordering primitives therefore leads to intermittent corruption, exactly the problem described.

**Option:** Use std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_seq_cst) only on the producer side after writing the payload, without any ordering on the consumer side. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is incorrect. A full sequential‑consistent fence on the producer alone does not prevent the consumer from reading the index before the fence has taken effect; the consumer also needs an acquire operation to synchronize with the producer's release. Omitting the acquire side leaves a gap where the consumer may observe the new index while still seeing old payload data.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of memory‑ordering requirements for lock‑free single‑producer/single‑consumer ring buffers on weakly‑ordered CPUs. The correct answer (option 1) highlights the need for a release store by the producer and an acquire load by the consumer, which together create a happens‑before relationship guaranteeing that the consumer sees a fully written message. Options 2, 4, and 5 confuse compiler‑level visibility (volatile, padding) with hardware memory ordering, a common mistake that leads to subtle bugs. Option 3 suggests using mutexes, which would meet correctness but catastrophically degrade the strict latency and throughput goals. Option 6 places a fence only on one side, ignoring the symmetric acquire needed on the consumer, another frequent misconception. In practice, developers should use C11 atomic types with `memory_order_release` and `memory_order_acquire` or explicit barrier intrinsics, and still consider cache‑line padding for performance, but never rely solely on `volatile` or assume ordering without explicit primitives.

### Question 87 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Employ a lock‑free single‑producer/single‑consumer ring buffer (e. g., DPDK rte_ring) that passes only a pointer to a pre‑allocated packet buffer together with a lightweight metadata struct, avoiding any per‑packet allocation or copy.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Allocate a new buffer for each packet in every stage and pass the buffer via a mutex‑protected FIFO queue, copying the packet metadata each time. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Allocating a fresh buffer for every packet introduces dynamic memory operations in the hot path, which are costly and may cause fragmentation, violating the zero‑drop requirement. The mutex also adds lock contention, increasing latency especially at 10 Gbps throughput.

**Option:** Use POSIX message queues to send the entire packet payload and metadata between stages, performing a memcpy on each send. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. POSIX message queues copy the data they transport, so each stage would incur a full packet memcpy, dramatically raising latency and CPU usage. Additionally, message queues are not designed for the ultra‑low latency, high‑throughput demands of line‑rate packet processing.

**Option:** Employ a lock‑free single‑producer/single‑consumer ring buffer (e. g., DPDK rte_ring) that passes only a pointer to a pre‑allocated packet buffer together with a lightweight metadata struct, avoiding any per‑packet allocation or copy. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. A lock‑free ring buffer enables producers and consumers to enqueue/dequeue pointers without locks, eliminating contention and keeping the critical path deterministic. By using a pool of pre‑allocated buffers, no dynamic memory allocation occurs in the hot path, and only a small metadata structure is transferred, meeting the zero‑drop and latency goals.

**Option:** Create a shared memory segment and use condition variables to synchronize access, but allocate a fresh metadata structure for each packet before enqueueing. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While shared memory avoids copying the packet payload, allocating a new metadata structure per packet re‑introduces dynamic allocation overhead. Condition variables also involve kernel transitions, which add latency unsuitable for line‑rate processing.

**Option:** Transmit packets between stages over TCP sockets bound to localhost, sending the metadata as part of the TCP stream. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. TCP adds protocol processing, buffering, and copy overhead, which are far too heavyweight for intra‑process communication on a single server. The extra latency and context switches would prevent achieving zero packet loss at 10 Gbps.

**Option:** Use a global array of packet descriptors protected by a spinlock, copying the descriptor to the next stage each time. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Even though a spinlock is faster than a mutex, it still creates contention when many cores try to acquire it simultaneously. Copying the descriptor per stage adds unnecessary memory traffic, and the lock can become a bottleneck under line‑rate loads.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests the learner's understanding of low‑latency, lock‑free inter‑thread communication in high‑performance packet processing. The optimal solution is a lock‑free ring buffer that passes only pointers to pre‑allocated buffers, eliminating dynamic allocation and memory copies in the hot path. Common misconceptions include believing that mutexes, condition variables, or TCP sockets provide sufficient performance; in reality, they introduce copying, kernel transitions, or lock contention that impair line‑rate processing. Even shared memory alone is insufficient if per‑packet allocations or heavyweight synchronization are used. Best practice is to allocate a buffer pool at startup, use a lock‑free queue (e. g., DPDK rte_ring), and transfer minimal metadata alongside a pointer, ensuring deterministic latency and zero packet drops.

### Question 88 Explanation

**Correct Answers:**
1. Define an enum that lists all valid keys and write a lookup function that converts a parsed string to the corresponding enum value; then use a switch statement on the enum for runtime handling.

2. Use an X‑macro that lists every key once and expands to both an enum and a parallel array of string literals, then map the parsed string to the enum via a generated binary‑search or switch routine.

3. Generate a perfect hash function with a tool like gperf from the known key list; the generated function returns an enum constant for a matching string and any undefined key reference fails to compile.

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Define an enum that lists all valid keys and write a lookup function that converts a parsed string to the corresponding enum value; then use a switch statement on the enum for runtime handling. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This approach is correct because the enum provides a compile‑time list of identifiers; any misspelled enum name used elsewhere will cause a compilation error. The conversion function can be generated from the same enum definition, guaranteeing consistency. At runtime the switch compiles to a series of integer comparisons, which are extremely fast.

**Option:** Create #define macros for each key (e. g., #define LOG_LEVEL_DEBUG 0) and compare the file strings to the macro names using strcmp at runtime. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Although #define creates integer constants, the macro names are not used as identifiers when comparing strings, so a typo in the source code will not be detected by the compiler. Moreover, strcmp incurs a full string comparison for every lookup, which is slower than integer‑based dispatch.

**Option:** Use an X‑macro that lists every key once and expands to both an enum and a parallel array of string literals, then map the parsed string to the enum via a generated binary‑search or switch routine. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This method is correct because the single source of truth (the X‑macro) guarantees that the enum and the string table stay in sync, and any reference to a non‑existent enum constant triggers a compile‑time error. The generated mapping code can be implemented as a switch or binary search, both of which reduce to integer comparisons after the string has been resolved. It also scales well when new keys are added, because only the X‑macro list needs updating.

**Option:** Build a runtime hash table (for example, using uthash) that stores the key strings and their associated integer constants, and look up each file key at execution time. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This answer is incorrect. A runtime hash table provides fast average‑case lookups, but it does not give any compile‑time checking of key names; misspelled identifiers in the source code will compile fine but may cause logic errors. Additionally, constructing the hash table at startup adds overhead that is unnecessary when the key set is fixed and known.

**Option:** Generate a perfect hash function with a tool like gperf from the known key list; the generated function returns an enum constant for a matching string and any undefined key reference fails to compile. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. A perfect hash produced by gperf yields a deterministic O(1) lookup that directly maps a string to an enum value, and the generated code includes a static switch on the enum, ensuring integer‑based comparison. Because the enum constants are defined in the same generated header, using a misspelled constant results in a compilation error, satisfying the requirement for compile‑time typo detection.

**Option:** Read each line into a struct of fixed‑size char arrays and compare the key field with hard‑coded string literals using strcmp for every lookup. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This choice is incorrect. While simple to implement, it relies on repeated strcmp calls, which are slower than integer comparisons and provides no compile‑time validation of the literal names. A typo in a literal will not be caught until runtime, potentially leading to silent configuration errors.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests the ability to enforce compile‑time validation of a known set of configuration keys while still achieving fast runtime dispatch. Using enums, X‑macros, or a perfect‑hash generator creates a single authoritative list of keys; any misspelled identifier used in code will cause a compilation error, preventing subtle bugs. These techniques also allow the parser to translate a string from the configuration file into an enum and then handle it with a switch or other integer‑based logic, which is far more efficient than repeated string comparisons. Common misconceptions include relying on #define macros or runtime hash tables, both of which miss the compile‑time safety guarantee and often incur unnecessary overhead. In production code, consolidating key definitions via X‑macros or code‑generating tools like gperf is considered best practice for maintainability and performance.

### Question 89 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Fixed‑point arithmetic executes in a constant number of cycles and typically fits within the 2 ms budget, while software floating‑point emulation can require many more cycles and may exceed the deadline.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Fixed‑point uses more memory than floating‑point emulation, so the DSP will run out of RAM before completing the frame. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is incorrect. Fixed‑point arithmetic actually reduces memory usage because values are stored as scaled integers rather than 64‑bit doubles. The primary constraint on the DSP in this scenario is CPU cycle budget, not RAM, so memory consumption is not the key differentiator.

**Option:** Floating‑point emulation yields higher numeric precision than fixed‑point, allowing the radar to meet its detection accuracy without any code changes. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** While software emulation can provide IEEE‑754 precision, the critical issue here is execution speed, not raw numeric precision. Fixed‑point can be designed with enough bits to meet the required accuracy, but the advantage of floating‑point emulation is outweighed by its heavy CPU cost. Therefore, the claim that precision alone makes it the better choice is a common misconception.

**Option:** Fixed‑point arithmetic executes in a constant number of cycles and typically fits within the 2 ms budget, while software floating‑point emulation can require many more cycles and may exceed the deadline. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This is the correct answer. Fixed‑point operations are integer‑based and deterministic, giving predictable latency that can be tightly bounded to meet real‑time constraints. In contrast, floating‑point emulation involves multiple integer operations per FP operation, leading to variable and often much larger cycle counts that risk violating the 2‑ms frame.

**Option:** Fixed‑point code automatically benefits from the DSP’s SIMD instructions, whereas floating‑point emulation cannot be vectorized. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is incorrect. SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) capabilities are available for both integer and software‑emulated floating‑point operations, provided the programmer uses the appropriate intrinsics or compiler flags. Fixed‑point does not inherently obtain SIMD acceleration without explicit coding, so the statement overstates the advantage.

**Option:** Using floating‑point emulation eliminates the need to scale values, which reduces the risk of overflow compared to fixed‑point. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is a misconception. Although floating‑point representation handles a wide dynamic range, emulated operations can still overflow if the exponent exceeds representable limits, and the software must still guard against it. Fixed‑point requires explicit scaling, but that scaling is a controlled design step that can prevent overflow as well, so risk is not eliminated by choosing emulation.

**Option:** Fixed‑point arithmetic guarantees bit‑exact results across different compiler versions, while floating‑point emulation may produce slightly different rounding on each build. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is not accurate. Both fixed‑point and software‑emulated floating‑point can be made deterministic if the same library and compiler options are used. Differences in rounding usually arise from library implementation choices, not from the arithmetic format itself, making this a common but false belief.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of performance versus precision trade‑offs on a DSP lacking a hardware FPU. The key difference is that fixed‑point arithmetic operates with predictable integer cycles, allowing the 2‑ms deadline to be met, whereas floating‑point emulation incurs substantial and variable overhead that can breach the timing budget. Many learners mistakenly focus on memory usage, precision, or automatic SIMD benefits, but those are secondary to the deterministic execution time requirement. Fixed‑point also requires careful scaling, but this is a design task rather than a performance penalty. In real‑world radar or communications DSPs, engineers often convert critical loops to fixed‑point to guarantee latency, using software‑floating point only for non‑time‑critical code.

### Question 90 Explanation

**Correct Answers:**
1. Define the protocol‑buffer structs with `__attribute__((packed))` (or an equivalent `#pragma pack`) and use `memcpy` to read/write individual fields instead of directly dereferencing potentially unaligned pointers.

2. Replace all raw integer types with fixed‑width types from `<stdint. h>` and apply explicit byte‑order conversion (e. g., `htobe32`, `be32toh`) when reading from or writing to memory‑mapped registers and protocol buffers.

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Change all pointer arithmetic expressions from `int *` to `long *` to match the 64‑bit word size, assuming that this will automatically fix alignment issues. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Alignment requirements are determined by the natural alignment of the type being accessed, not by the size of the pointer used for arithmetic. Switching to `long *` may actually increase the stride and introduce new misalignments, and it does not address the need for explicit packing or byte‑order handling.

**Option:** Define the protocol‑buffer structs with `__attribute__((packed))` (or an equivalent `#pragma pack`) and use `memcpy` to read/write individual fields instead of directly dereferencing potentially unaligned pointers. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. Marking the structs as packed tells the compiler not to insert padding, preserving the exact layout required by the binary protocol. Using `memcpy` avoids undefined behavior that can arise from accessing unaligned data through a pointer, which is essential on platforms with strict alignment like 64‑bit Linux.

**Option:** Compile the program with the `-mno-align` flag to tell GCC to ignore alignment requirements on the target platform. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because such a flag does not exist in GCC, and even if it did, ignoring hardware alignment would lead to bus errors or corrupted data. Alignment is enforced by the CPU, not by the compiler, so the code must be written to respect it. Attempting to bypass alignment would make the program non‑portable and unsafe.

**Option:** Cast the base hardware register address to a `uint64_t *` and read/write 64‑bit values directly, assuming the hardware will handle the conversion. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. The original hardware registers are typically 32‑bit wide, and accessing them as 64‑bit may generate misaligned accesses or unintended side effects such as combining two registers into one read. Moreover, the hardware does not automatically perform byte‑order conversion; doing so without explicit handling can corrupt the data stream.

**Option:** Replace all raw integer types with fixed‑width types from `<stdint. h>` and apply explicit byte‑order conversion (e. g., `htobe32`, `be32toh`) when reading from or writing to memory‑mapped registers and protocol buffers. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. Fixed‑width types give a clear guarantee about the number of bits, which is crucial when moving between 32‑bit and 64‑bit environments. Explicit endian conversion ensures that data is interpreted correctly on a platform with different byte ordering, preventing subtle bugs that arise from assuming the same endian as the source hardware.

**Option:** Add `#define LITTLE_ENDIAN` at the top of the source files to force the compiler to treat the target as little‑endian, thereby avoiding the need for byte‑order swaps. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Endianness is a property of the processor architecture and cannot be overridden by a preprocessor macro; the compiler will still generate code for the actual hardware's byte order. Without proper conversion functions, data transferred to or from big‑endian devices will be misinterpreted, leading to corrupted values and protocol failures.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of data‑layout portability when moving code from a 32‑bit, possibly little‑endian, embedded system to a 64‑bit, possibly big‑endian, Linux server. The key issues are strict alignment requirements and differing byte order, both of which require explicit handling in portable C code. Using `__attribute__((packed))` together with `memcpy` (option 2) avoids undefined behavior caused by unaligned accesses, while employing fixed‑width integer types and explicit endian conversion functions (option 5) guarantees that the program interprets binary data consistently across architectures. The incorrect options reflect common misconceptions: that simply changing pointer types fixes alignment, that compiler flags can disable hardware constraints, that casting to larger integer types magically handles register size, or that a macro can change the CPU's endianness. Best practice is to design data structures with explicit packing, use safe memory‑copy techniques for unaligned data, and always perform endian conversion when crossing architectural boundaries.

### Question 91 Explanation

**Correct Answers:**
1. Convert all multi-byte integer fields from network byte order to host byte order using ntohs/ntohl after reading them from the raw buffer.

2. Declare the header structures with a packed attribute (e. g., __attribute__((packed))) or appropriate #pragma pack directives to prevent compiler‑added padding.

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Convert all multi-byte integer fields from network byte order to host byte order using ntohs/ntohl after reading them from the raw buffer. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. Network protocols define multi-byte fields in big‑endian (network) order, so a little‑endian host must swap bytes while a big‑endian host must not. Using ntohs/ntohl (or similar macros) guarantees that the values are interpreted consistently on any architecture, eliminating the observed discrepancy.

**Option:** Declare the header structures with a packed attribute (e. g., __attribute__((packed))) or appropriate #pragma pack directives to prevent compiler‑added padding. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. When overlaying a union on a raw byte buffer, any compiler‑added padding would shift fields and cause misinterpretation of the packet layout, especially on platforms with different alignment rules. Marking the structures as packed forces the layout to match the on‑the‑wire format, making the union overlay reliable across endian variants.

**Option:** Rely on the union to automatically handle endianness, because the same memory is shared between the raw buffer and the header structures. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A union merely provides overlapping storage; it does not perform byte swapping or alter the order of bytes. Without explicit conversion, the multi-byte fields will be read in the host's native order, leading to wrong values on a big‑endian system.

**Option:** Use the enumeration value directly as an index into an array of function pointers without any bounds checking. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While using an enum to select a handler function is common, skipping bounds checks can cause out‑of‑range accesses and undefined behavior, but it does not address the endian problem described. The test failure is unrelated to function dispatch logic.

**Option:** Store the raw packet buffer as an array of uint32_t and cast it to the union type to improve performance. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Casting a uint32_t array to a union of packed structures can violate alignment requirements on some architectures and exacerbates endian issues, because each uint32_t would already be in network order. This practice can cause misaligned accesses and further corrupt the parsed data.

**Option:** Assume that the little‑endian development machine and the big‑endian target have the same representation for bitfields, so keep the existing bitfield definitions unchanged. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. The layout of bitfields is implementation‑defined and can differ not only with endianness but also with compiler settings. Assuming identical representation leads to incorrect extraction of flag bits on the big‑endian platform, contributing to the observed errors.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of data representation issues that arise when parsing network packets on platforms with different byte orders. Network protocols specify fields in big‑endian (network) order, so software must explicitly translate multi-byte integers with ntohs/ntohl or similar functions; failing to do so yields wrong values on big‑endian targets where no swap occurs. Additionally, overlaying structs on a raw byte buffer via a union requires the structs to have exactly the same layout as the on‑the‑wire format; compiler‑added padding can shift fields, so using packed attributes or pragma directives is essential. Common misconceptions include believing that a union automatically resolves endianness or that bitfield layouts are portable, both of which are false and lead to subtle bugs. Best practice is to treat the wire format as a sequence of bytes, copy them into packed structs with memcpy, and apply explicit byte‑order conversions for every multi-byte field before use.

### Question 92 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** Apply a compiler pragma or attribute (e. g., #pragma pack or __attribute__((packed))) to force the struct to have the same layout and size as on the 32-bit platform.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Apply a compiler pragma or attribute (e. g., #pragma pack or __attribute__((packed))) to force the struct to have the same layout and size as on the 32-bit platform. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This is the correct first step because the immediate problem is a mismatch in the in‑memory layout caused by different alignment rules on the two ABIs. By packing the struct you eliminate the extra padding that the 64‑bit compiler inserts for pointer fields, making the binary representation match the original protocol. Once the layout matches, the existing parsing code will read the correct offsets, preserving compatibility without a large redesign.

**Option:** Change all int fields in the struct to int64_t so they match the size of pointers on the 64-bit platform. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because increasing the size of integer fields will further diverge the struct layout from the 32‑bit definition, breaking the wire protocol rather than fixing it. The protocol expects 32‑bit integers; using 64‑bit types would add extra bytes and shift subsequent fields. Moreover, the size mismatch is caused by pointer alignment, not by the width of int fields.

**Option:** Recompile the entire program with the -m32 flag to force 32-bit code generation on the x86-64 machine. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Compiling as 32‑bit would indeed produce the same struct size, but it defeats the purpose of moving to a 64‑bit platform and introduces other compatibility and performance issues. It is a heavyweight workaround that does not address the root cause of relying on native struct layout for a network protocol. The requirement is to keep the application 64‑bit while preserving the on‑wire format, so this is not the appropriate first action.

**Option:** Replace the binary protocol with a JSON‑based format to avoid issues with struct padding and alignment. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** While moving to a text‑based format eliminates binary layout concerns, it is an extensive redesign that goes far beyond the immediate need for compatibility. Changing the whole protocol would require coordinated updates on all clients and servers, breaking existing 32‑bit clients. Therefore, it is not the first step; a simpler fix to the struct layout should be attempted first.

**Option:** Add runtime checks using sizeof to verify the struct size on startup and abort if it differs from the expected 32‑bit size. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Runtime validation can alert developers to size mismatches, but it does not resolve the underlying problem of incorrect offsets in the protocol parsing. Simply aborting preserves compatibility at the cost of unavailable functionality, which is undesirable in production. The proper approach is to correct the layout so that the checks never fail.

**Option:** Refactor the parsing function to read each field individually using known byte offsets instead of relying on the struct layout. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Manually decoding fields based on explicit offsets is a robust long‑term solution, but it requires a substantial amount of code changes and careful handling of endianness. It is typically undertaken after the protocol format is formally defined, not as the first quick fix. Packing the struct provides an immediate remedy while a more thorough serialization layer can be introduced later.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The problem originates from differences in ABI-defined padding and alignment between 32‑bit ARM and 64‑bit x86‑64, which change the in‑memory size of a mixed-type struct. The most direct first remedy is to force the struct to use the original 32‑bit layout by applying a packing pragma or attribute, thereby matching the wire format expected by existing clients. Changing integer widths, recompiling as 32‑bit, or switching to a completely different protocol are either ineffective or overly disruptive solutions. Runtime size checks and complete refactoring of the parser are valuable later‑stage strategies but do not address the immediate compatibility issue. Best practice is to avoid sending raw structs over the network; instead, define an explicit on‑wire format with fixed‑width types and perform manual serialization, but the first practical step is to make the current struct layout compatible through packing.

### Question 93 Explanation

::: correctbox
**Correct Answer:** The stack uses a fixed-size array and overwrites the oldest entry when full, so incoming requests replace previously stored history.
:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** The stack uses a fixed-size array and overwrites the oldest entry when full, so incoming requests replace previously stored history. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. A fixed-size array cannot grow, and the overwrite-on-full policy deliberately discards older entries, leading to silent data loss. In a high‑traffic web server this means earlier request logs are lost as soon as the array reaches its limit, violating the requirement that no data be discarded.

**Option:** Because the data structure is LIFO, it automatically throws away the newest request when capacity is reached. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A stack (LIFO) removes the most recent element only when a pop operation occurs, not when the container is full. The loss described in the scenario originates from the overwrite policy, not from the intrinsic ordering semantics of a stack.

**Option:** Multiple threads push to the stack without any synchronization, causing race conditions that corrupt the stored entries. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While missing mutexes can indeed corrupt data, the question explicitly states that the implementation overwrites the oldest entry when the array is full. The primary cause of loss is the deliberate overwrite strategy, not concurrent access issues, although concurrency would be another bug to address.

**Option:** Using a stack instead of a queue reverses the order of request history, which makes the oldest entries appear first and thus seem lost. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Choosing a stack over a queue changes the retrieval order but does not by itself discard data. The problem described is about data being overwritten, not about ordering, so the root cause is unrelated to the LIFO vs FIFO choice.

**Option:** The implementation fails to wrap the index back to zero after reaching the end of the array, leading to out‑of‑bounds writes that corrupt memory. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. An out‑of‑bounds write would cause a crash or undefined behaviour, not the systematic loss of the oldest entry while staying within bounds. The described behavior is intentional overwriting, not an indexing error.

**Option:** The compiler optimizes away the array because it is never read after being written, so no data is ever actually stored. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Modern compilers will not eliminate a variable that may have side effects observable by other parts of the program, especially when its address could be taken. Even if optimization removed the array, the symptom would be missing data, not the specific pattern of overwriting older entries described in the scenario.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of capacity management in fixed-size data structures. The root cause of the observed data loss is the deliberate design choice to overwrite the oldest entry once the array is full, which violates the requirement that no data be silently discarded. Many candidates might mistakenly blame concurrency, indexing errors, or the LIFO nature of a stack, but those are separate concerns. In real-world systems, a stack used for request history should either be dynamically resized or paired with an explicit overflow handling strategy (e. g., refusing new pushes or using a circular buffer with a well‑defined eviction policy). Recognizing that fixed-size containers must be managed carefully prevents subtle data‑loss bugs in high‑throughput services.
